content:
Sessions keep skipping a recall your instructions ask for before each code change, and you use Claude Code. Try the instructions first: in Scatterhoard's own project, a paragraph in `AGENTS.md` carrying the habit and its settings was enough, and the nudge below rarely fired. If skips persist, write a small `PreToolUse` hook that reminds the session once per commit.
1. Read the JSON payload Claude Code sends on stdin. `tool_name` and `tool_input` say whether this call writes code: an edit tool's `file_path` under your code directories, or a Bash command that writes there.
2. Read the file at `transcript_path`, one JSON object per line. Scan the `tool_use` blocks for the last `git commit` and for a `hoard_recall` after it. Match the tool name by its `__hoard_recall` suffix, since the server's name varies by machine, and check the arguments your habit prescribes. A recall made for another purpose with the same arguments will still count.
3. If none is found, print `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "additionalContext": "<one line asking for the recall>"}}`. The model receives it; a person may not see it.
4. Keep a marker per `session_id` so it fires once per commit, log every decision, and exit 0 on any error, so the hook can never stop an edit.
5. Wire it in `.claude/settings.local.json` under `hooks.PreToolUse`, matcher `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash`, command the script's absolute path.
Check: make a code edit with no recall since your last commit; the log records a nudge and the session answers it. A second edit is not nudged.
context: Recording the recall nudge as an option after its two-week experiment, when the human partner asked for a recipe someone could build from rather than a link.
why: Built and run in Scatterhoard's own project for two weeks from 2026-10-05. Of 58 code writes it nudged twice, because the instruction paragraph already held the habit. So this is a fallback, not a step. It is written so that a competent author can build their own without the original script, which lives in a repository the reader may not have.

content:
Recall misses memories full of specialist terms borrowed from another language, such as an English set about Italian cooking, though it works for the rest. Measure how well the model reads the set's own vocabulary, then decide.
1. Store ten test memories in the set's scope, each carrying `hoard-fit-sentences` and the set's language keyword, such as `hoard-lang-en`. Each holds a JSON array of three sentences: an anchor using one of the terms, a paraphrase explaining it without the term, and a sentence on a topic none of the anchors touch. For example: Test 1. ["finish the risotto with a proper mantecatura", "at the end, beat cold butter and grated cheese into the rice until it turns creamy", "the oven needs fifteen minutes to preheat"]
2. Link all ten from the set's `hoard-fit-hub` memory with `refers_to` links. Write the hub if the set has none, or supersede it to add them.
3. `hoard_sets` action `status` now scores that language from these sentences, 0 to 10, in `language_scores`.
4. To try another model, set `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` to it in the client's server configuration, restart, run `hoard_sets` action `reembed` for the set, and read the score again.
5. If a model scores clearly higher, record it as a recommendation. If none does, give each such memory its terms as keywords: keyword recall matches them exactly under any model.
Check: the score appears in `language_scores`. Measured once, Italian kitchen terms scored 1 of 10 under potion-base-32M and 2 under potion-multilingual-128M, so a better model is not guaranteed.
context: Writing the cookbook recipes for set-carried model recommendations and a set's own test sentences, the day both were built.
why: Run end to end on 2026-10-04 against a disposable home with the real server, both models and ten Italian-kitchen triplets, including the switch, the re-embed and a keyword recall finding a term the semantic path missed.

content: This set holds recipes for people using Scatterhoard: how to get something done with it, written for a session that has a goal or a symptom in front of it and no copy of Scatterhoard's repository. A memory belongs here when it is a procedure a user can follow on their own machine and their own sets — setting up, moving data, recovering from a mistake, building for themselves something Scatterhoard's project built for its own use — and when that procedure has been run end to end before it was written. Each recipe opens with the reader's goal or symptom, in the words a session would use to ask for it. Why Scatterhoard is designed as it is belongs with Scatterhoard's own set; a recipe says what to do, and what to check to know it worked.
context: Creating the scatterhoard-cookbook set, right after making absorb merge a split personal store; its first recipes are moving the data directories and recovering from a move that went wrong.
why: The charter, approved by the human partner 2026-09-30 when the set was created, settling `where-user-facing-recipes-live` in Scatterhoard's own set. The audience is a user's session, which has no repository, so the routing test is whether the procedure needs one. Run-end-to-end is stated here rather than only in a design document, because the charter is the one text every writer to this set recalls, and it is what keeps an untested recipe out. What-to-check makes verification part of every recipe. Reasoning stays with Scatterhoard's own set so a design change cannot silently stale a recipe's explanation.

It applied the seven flagging conditions in `documents/design/export-review.md` as committed alongside this marker, with no private-only exceptions in force, since the repository is going public. A routine review starts from the export this marker is committed with.

content:
Moving your personal memory to another directory. Your personal memory is the `local` set, one file, `local.sqlite3`, in the directory `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` names; unset, that is `SCATTERHOARD_HOME`, and unset in turn, `~/.local/share/scatterhoard`. On Windows, set `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` yourself.
1. Call `hoard_sets` action `status` and note `local`'s `file`, `set_id` and `memories`.
2. Stop every client that runs Scatterhoard: each starts its own server.
3. Move `local.sqlite3` into the new directory. It is the whole store; nothing beside it needs to move.
4. Set `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` to the new directory in every client's server configuration. A client left without it reads the old place, finds nothing, and starts a second, empty personal store.
5. Start the clients again.
Check: `status` shows `local`'s `file` in the new directory, with the same `set_id` and `memories` as in step 1. A missing or different `set_id` means a server is reading a new, empty store: see the recipe for personal memories that seem to have disappeared.
context: The first recipe, written when the set was created, from Scatterhoard's issue about a moved personal store leaving the old one unmentioned.
why: Run end to end on 2026-09-30 against a disposable home with the real server and model: the moved store kept its identity and every memory, and recall found them.

content:
You want everyone who uses a set to know which embedding model to load: you found one that serves the set better than the default. Record it in the set itself, so it travels with every copy.
1. Find the set's hub: `hoard_recall` with `keywords` ["hoard-fit-hub"] and the set's `scope`. If there is none, store one: a short memory in that scope carrying only the keyword `hoard-fit-hub`, such as "This set's model-fit hub." Note the hub's id. A set has one hub.
2. Store the recommendation in the same set: a memory carrying `hoard-fit-model`, whose opening sentence names the model and what it does better, because status shows only that line. Give it a `refers_to` link to the hub's id, and a `hoard-lang-` keyword for each language you measured it on, or none if it concerns the whole set. Say how you measured it.
3. Export and commit the set as usual, so the recommendation reaches everyone else's copy.
Check: `hoard_sets` action `status` lists it under the set's `recommended_models`, with its id, opening line and languages. A refusal saying the memory links to no hub means the link is missing or points elsewhere; the refusal names the hub to link to, or shows how to write one.
context: Writing the cookbook recipes for set-carried model recommendations and a set's own test sentences, the day both were built.
why: Run end to end on 2026-10-04 against a disposable home with the real server: a hub, then a linked recommendation, and status listed it. gemma4:12b followed the same steps from status's own note 10 times in 10.
The name this set attributes writes to. Held as a memory so that changing it supersedes one record rather than rewriting every record that names it.

content: Every time you finish a change, writing the memories about it means another review and export before you can commit, and then that round needs recording too, so the work never seems to reach zero. Close a change in this order instead. 1. Finish the code and get its checks passing. 2. Store every memory the change owes: what you decided, what is worth remembering, and anything that marks the work done, since the work is done once the checks pass and the commit only records it. 3. Run the export review once, with `hoard_sets` action `review`, over everything waiting, and answer it with `clear`. 4. Export the set with `hoard_sets` action `export`, then read the memory file's diff and the description the export returns. 5. Regenerate anything your project builds from the exported file. 6. Commit. Anything you learn after the commit stays in the store for the next one: the next session start lists it under `review_due`, so do not chase an empty store. Never write a memory that can only be true after the commit, such as one naming the commit's hash; name a commit by its date and subject. **To check it worked:** the export reports only this change's memories as new, nothing waits in `review_due` for this change, and `git status` is clean after the commit.
context: Closing out the export review's judgement gate, the first change closed in this order.
why: Run end to end on Scatterhoard's own set on 2026-10-26: storing "the work is built" after an export had needed a second review and export, and a memory recording that would have needed a third. In this order, one review covered both closing memories, one export added only those two, and the commit left nothing over. The reasoning is in Scatterhoard's own set, under `closing-a-change`.

content:
Your personal memories seem to have disappeared: recall finds nothing you remember storing, or `local` reports fewer memories than it should. Usually nothing is lost. This server is reading a different `local.sqlite3` from the one they are in, because `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` or `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` changed, or differs between clients.
1. Call `hoard_sets` action `status`. `local`'s `file` is the store being read; a `set_id` that is missing, or differs from one you noted before, means it is not your usual store.
2. Find the old store: look for `local.sqlite3` in the directories the variables named before, and in `~/.local/share/scatterhoard`.
3. If the store being read holds memories written since, keep them: call action `export` with scope `local` and a `file` outside any `scatterhoard_mem`.
4. Stop every client, and move the old `local.sqlite3` over the one being read.
5. Start one client. If you exported in step 3, call action `absorb` with scope `local`, that `file`, and a `save_to` path for a safety copy.
6. Make every client's configuration agree, so this does not happen again.
Check: `status` shows `local` with its old `set_id`, and `memories` counting both stores. Absorbing the same file twice changes nothing.
context: The second recipe, written when the set was created, after running the recovery found and fixed absorb's refusal of a local file.
why: Run end to end on 2026-09-30 on a disposable home: a memory written into the wrong store came back under the original identity. Needs a Scatterhoard release whose `absorb` takes a `local` file into `local`.
